title: How to Analyze Banks (Part 2): Deposits, Valuations, and Silicon Valley
summary: Eisman explains deposit franchises, SVB's duration and funding failure, bank income statements and tangible-book valuation. He favors large banks but avoids adding them at rich valuations and with AI financing exposure. The central SVB mechanism and conditional arithmetic are useful. Material errors concern securities accounting, liquidity-rule maturity restrictions, SVB closure timing and OZK consumer lending. Current credit data is broadly stable, but not uniformly benign. Claims of zero systemic risk and inevitable consolidation are substantially less established.
assessment: A useful bank-analysis framework with several consequential factual and accounting simplifications. Distinguish book, regulatory and economic capital; liquidity from duration; and reported returns from stock-valuation judgments. The solo presentation means all extracted substantive views are Eisman's.
speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_00 self-identifies as Steve Eisman at the beginning and delivers the entire solo tutorial.
framework_points: Analyze deposit composition and correlation, not merely total balances.
Separate funding cost, asset duration and credit risk.
Decompose pre-provision earnings from credit provisions.
Compare tangible-book multiples with sustainable returns and cost of equity.
Treat good valuation logic as insufficient to predict merger execution.
Assess indirect portfolio exposure through investment-banking clients.
tools_and_charts: Net interest margin and earning assets
SVB deposits, securities marks and VC funding chronology
Q2 2026 large-bank ROTCE and price/tangible-book table
transcript_cautions: SVB and SIVB refer to bank and holding-company ticker; their asset totals and capital measures differ.
Captions name Basel IV endgame; the official proposal is Basel III endgame.
The spoken JPMorgan quarter and $16.9 billion figure do not match the inspected Q1 release; charts are not included in the text.
Bank of the Ozarks is the former name of Bank OZK; no-consumer lending is a substantive false claim, not a harmless name correction.
The spoken flat/nonaccrual generalization does not include a bank-by-bank data table in the transcript.

claims.claim: Stable deposits can let a bank hold performing bonds to maturity, making duration losses an income problem instead of a forced-sale crisis.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Evaluate funding persistence, capital, collateral capacity and contractual repayment.
claims.reason: Holding avoids crystallizing a market discount if payments arrive; stability alone does not remove economic capital loss, negative carry or every solvency risk.
claims.next_check: Evaluate funding persistence, capital, collateral capacity and contractual repayment.
claims.deductive_proof: Assume contractual bond payments are made, deposits remain available through maturity, and all other cash obligations can be met. With no required sale, the bank collects contractual principal and coupons rather than selling at the lower market price. However, present value still falls when the discount rate rises, and stable deposits alone do not prove the other liquidity or solvency assumptions. Thus the conditional funding insight is valid but incomplete as a general solvency claim.

proof.derivation: Assume contractual bond payments are made, deposits remain available through maturity, and all other cash obligations can be met. claims.claim: Higher sustainable return on tangible equity generally supports a higher price-to-tangible-book ratio.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Apply a steady-state residual-income or dividend model with equal growth and cost of equity.
claims.qualifications: Holds growth and cost of equity constant; real bank differences can dominate.
claims.reason: With constant growth g and equity cost r greater than g, justified P/B=(ROE-g)/(r-g), increasing in ROE when other inputs are fixed. This is a conditional model, not every bank's observed price.
